consensus_summary: The recognizable majority interpretation identifies lamp oil with the Holy Spirit or His sustaining grace, while also acknowledging readiness, genuine faith, and good works or obedient discipleship as established alternatives.
book_summary: The book explicitly denies that the oil is the Spirit Himself and instead identifies it as the accumulated, tested fruit and evidence of the Spirit’s work—proven obedience that is stored and consumed to produce visible light.
rationale: This materially displaces the dominant Spirit identification, so it is divergent rather than merely refined. Nevertheless, it is not novel: the blind responses recognize good works, obedience, persevering discipleship, and inward spiritual fruit as traditional alternatives. The book sharpens that family of readings by distinguishing the Spirit as cause from obedient fruit as the oil produced.
strongest_objection: The cited texts support several components—Ezekiel 36:27 connects the indwelling Spirit with obedience; Matthew 5:16 connects light with good works; Proverbs 21:20 and Matthew 25 associate retained oil with wisdom and preparedness. But none explicitly identifies lamp oil as accumulated, proven obedience, and Matthew 25 does not decode the oil. Zechariah 4:6 may instead favor the common Spirit association, while the language of pressed or tested fruit is largely inferred from the physical production of beaten olive oil.
